title: IF HE CHOSE ANOTHER WOMAN, GOD SAID HE STILL COULDN’T NEGLECT HER — The Forgotten Law in Exodus 21 That Reveals Something Powerful About the Heart of God
paragraphs: IF HE CHOSE ANOTHER WOMAN, GOD SAID HE STILL COULDN’T NEGLECT HER — The Forgotten Law in Exodus 21 That Reveals Something Powerful About the Heart of God

She lived in a world where powerful men could make decisions about her future. Yet buried inside an ancient law many Christians rush past, God placed words that restrained neglect—and declared that if her covenant provisions were denied, she could walk away free.
There are Bible verses we underline because they comfort us.
There are verses we memorize because they inspire us.
And then there are verses like Exodus 21:10–11.
Verses that make modern readers uncomfortable.
Verses that come from a world painfully different from ours.
Verses that should never be ripped from their historical setting, romanticized, or turned into something they are not.
But if you stay with this passage long enough…
Not because ancient Israel suddenly looks like twenty-first-century society.
Not because slavery was somehow beautiful.
Not because polygamy becomes God's ideal for marriage simply because the Old Testament regulates situations in which it existed.
In a social world where a vulnerable woman's future could be determined by people with far more power than she possessed, God's law placed obligations upon the powerful.
אִם־אַחֶרֶת יִקַּח־לוֹ שְׁאֵרָהּ כְּסוּתָהּ וְעֹנָתָהּ לֹא יִגְרָע
Im acheret yiqqach-lo, she'erah, kesutah, ve'onatah lo yigra.
If he takes another woman for himself, he must not diminish the first woman's food, clothing, or marital rights.
He could not simply replace her emotionally and then pretend she no longer mattered.
He could not take another wife and use that decision as permission to starve the first.
He could not stop clothing her.
He could not simply erase the obligations attached to her position.
Three Hebrew expressions stand there like witnesses:

That final word, עֹנָה (onah), is unusually rare in the Hebrew Bible and has generated scholarly discussion, but the traditional understanding reflected in many major translations is the woman's conjugal or marital right. Ancient interpretive traditions likewise understood the expression sexually or in terms of cohabitation.
the law was not merely concerned with whether she remained technically attached to a household.
The sentence that changes the emotional temperature of the entire passage.
If those obligations were not fulfilled…
No final invoice placed into the hands of the woman who had already been deprived.
Sit with that for a moment.
Because some people know what it feels like to be technically “kept” while emotionally abandoned.
but crying where nobody could see you.
because explaining the truth felt harder than carrying it.
Maybe someone didn't physically abandon you.
They just slowly stopped seeing you.
And sometimes neglect wounds differently from rejection because rejection at least announces itself.
Neglect makes you wonder whether you're unreasonable for hurting.
Maybe that's why this ancient sentence can hit so hard.
“Her food, her clothing, and her marital rights he shall not diminish.”
Do not treat her existence as though another person's arrival made her disposable.
And we need to be careful here.
Exodus 21 is civil legislation given to ancient Israel. We should not pretend every regulation in Israel's covenant law transfers directly into modern civil law or modern marriage practice.
Nor should we claim that this passage presents slavery or polygamy as God's creational ideal.
Back before human hearts twisted relationships into competitions for power.
When questioned about marriage, Christ pointed toward God's design “from the beginning.”
And Scripture ultimately points beyond every human marriage to something even greater: Christ and His people.
That is where this ancient law begins whispering something that eventually becomes thunder.
God notices how vulnerable people are treated.
Desire does not cancel covenant obligation.
And another person's arrival does not suddenly give you permission to dehumanize someone who depended upon your faithfulness.
The Bible is painfully realistic about human sin.
It doesn't even hide the failures of its heroes.
Jacob's household became tangled in rivalry.
David's sexual sin produced devastating consequences.
Solomon's marriages pulled his heart toward idolatry.
But scandal never gets the final word.
And that is where this story becomes ours.
Because maybe nobody ever sold you into an ancient household.
Maybe Exodus 21 describes a social world thousands of years removed from yours.
But you know what it means to need mercy.
Because beneath our different stories lies the same catastrophe.
But none of us escapes the diagnosis:
And the most terrifying slavery described by the Gospel isn't ultimately slavery to another human being.
Jesus said that everyone who practices sin is a slave to sin.
That means our deepest problem cannot be solved merely by becoming more disciplined.
And this is where the Gospel becomes almost unbearably beautiful.
Jesus Christ did not come merely to improve enslaved sinners.
The Son of God stepped into our broken world.
He spoke with women others despised.
Then He walked toward a cross carrying sins that were not His.
The hands that never committed evil were pierced.
The mouth that never lied tasted suffering.
The One who never betrayed the Father was treated as condemned.
And while human beings were doing their worst…
That means your scandal does not have sovereign authority over your ending.
Your religious performance doesn't save you either.
But grace is not permission to keep hugging the sin that nailed Christ to the cross.
Repentance means we stop defending what God calls sin and turn toward the Savior who receives sinners.
Maybe that's why you're still reading.
Maybe somewhere between an ancient Hebrew law and these words, God touched the place you've kept hidden.
Maybe you know what it's like to be neglected.
you're realizing you have been the one doing the neglecting.
Maybe you've been demanding faithfulness while refusing to give it.
Maybe someone living under your roof has been starving for tenderness while you've been feeding everyone else your attention.
Maybe your spouse gets whatever energy remains after your phone, career, entertainment, friends, ministry, and ambitions have eaten first.
Maybe you haven't committed adultery physically…
but your marriage has been surviving on emotional leftovers.
And maybe the person God is confronting in this passage isn't the wounded person.
Mercy strong enough to expose you without destroying you.
Mercy strong enough to forgive you without lying to you.
Mercy strong enough to transform what shame told you could never change.
If this exposed something you've been hiding, you don't have to write your entire story publicly.
And if you've spent years pretending you're fine when you're not…
maybe today your confession is simply:
There are people reading the comments who need to discover they aren't the only ones fighting.
Your honesty may become somebody else's courage.
And if somebody came into your mind while reading this, don't just think about them.
Someone is wondering whether God still wants them after what they've done.
Someone believes their scandal became their identity.
Someone is one night away from giving up on prayer.
Someone needs to hear that Christ still redeems sinners.
Sometimes sharing the Gospel is as simple as refusing to let truth stop with you.
Because there may come a night when you need these words more than you need them today.
Scripture teaches voluntary Christian generosity: “not reluctantly or under compulsion,” because God loves cheerful giving.
But voluntary support can still become an act of Christian generosity.
Your support doesn't purchase God's blessing.
But Gospel ministry still requires people willing to give, serve, share, pray, create, distribute, and stand together.
So if you want to glorify God by helping biblical truth travel farther, consider supporting this work—not from guilt, fear, or spiritual pressure, but freely, prayerfully, and joyfully.
More free resources reaching hungry believers.
More wounded people hearing about grace.
More wandering people being called home.
More sinners hearing that Jesus Christ still saves.
Then do something that costs nothing.
Because Exodus 21 leaves us with an uncomfortable but unforgettable picture.
A vulnerable woman could not simply be pushed into the shadows because someone else became desirable.
And when those stipulated provisions were refused…
the law said she could walk free without paying for her freedom.
But the Gospel tells an even greater story.
You and I could never purchase our own redemption.
Jesus Christ paid the price sinners could never pay.
And when the Son sets you free…
you don't walk out because you finally became worthy.
You walk out because He was.
Maybe your own choices shattered things you would give anything to rebuild.
And the nail-scarred hand holding the pen has never lost its power to turn the darkest chapter toward redemption.
Your scandal may explain a chapter of your story—but only Jesus has the authority to write the ending.
